messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
Does completeness of (M, d) guarantee the intersection property? Suppose (M, d) is complete and (Fₙ) is a sequence of nonempty closed subsets with Fₙ₊₁ ⊂ Fₙ and diam Fₙ → 0. For each n, fix a point xₙ ∈ Fₙ, and observe that for m > n, d(xₘ, xₙ) ≤ diam Fₙ → 0, so (xₙ) is Cauchy. Completeness yields xₙ → x ∈ M, and since xₘ ∈ Fₙ₀ for all m ≥ n₀ while Fₙ₀ is closed, we get x ∈ Fₙ₀ for every n₀. Therefore x ∈ ⋂ₙ Fₙ, confirming the forward direction.

Does the intersection property, in turn, imply completeness? For a Cauchy sequence (xₙ) in M, define Fₙ = cl{xₖ : k ≥ n}; each Fₙ is nonempty, closed, nested, and satisfies diam Fₙ → 0. The property provides x ∈ ⋂ₙ Fₙ, and since d(xₘ, x) ≤ diam Fₙ < ε for all m ≥ N (with diam Fₙ < ε), we conclude xₙ → x.

Is it possible for the intersection to be empty when the space is incomplete? Indeed, in an incomplete space one can construct a Cauchy sequence (xₙ) with no limit, and the sets Fₙ = cl{xₖ : k ≥ n} then have empty intersection. Can we verify that this construction works in a concrete incomplete space? In (0,1) with the usual metric, the sequence xₙ = 1/n is Cauchy but has no limit in (0,1), and the corresponding closed sets Fₙ = [1/n, 1) have diam → 0 yet ⋂ₙ Fₙ = ∅.
